intro: Hi Ahmed! Today you are on a mission in the Kitchen Lab. You will find out what really happens when things change. Why does meat change colour when you cook it? Why does a balloon blow itself up? And at the end, you will learn to write all of it in the secret code of chemists: chemical equations. Start with the warm-up and just guess, even a wrong guess gets your brain ready. Then open the map, one branch at a time. Let's go!
b0: Branch one: physical or chemical? There is just one question that decides it: did a new substance form? Picture an ice cube in your juice. It melts and becomes water, but it is still water, still H two O. That is a physical change: only the state or the shape changed. Now picture toast that burns black. That black stuff is carbon, a brand new substance. That is a chemical change. Watch out for the traps. A candle melting is physical, but a candle burning is chemical, because the wax reacts with oxygen and makes carbon dioxide and water vapour. And sugar in water does not disappear. The water tastes sweet, so the sugar is still there. That is physical.
b1: Branch two: what happens inside a reaction? Think of LEGO. You have a LEGO car. You take it apart, brick by brick, and with exactly the same bricks you build a plane. Same bricks, totally new thing. A chemical reaction is just like that. The starting substances are called reactants. The bonds between their atoms break. Then the atoms rearrange, and new bonds form, making new substances called products. For example, methane and oxygen: their bonds break, and we get carbon dioxide and water. Remember this line: same atoms, new partners.
b2: Branch three: how do you know a reaction happened? You cannot see atoms, but a reaction always leaves clues, like a detective case. Your code is: Police Catch Gas Leaks. P is for precipitate: silver nitrate with sodium chloride makes a white solid that turns violet in sunlight. C is for colour change: zinc in blue copper sulphate, the blue disappears and reddish-brown copper appears. G is for gas: magnesium in dilute acid makes hydrogen bubbles, and baking soda with vinegar makes carbon dioxide. L is for light and heat: burning magnesium gives a very bright light and heat. That is why you need tongs and a mask.
b3: Branch four: writing equations. An equation is like a recipe card in code. The ingredients go on the left, the dish goes on the right, and the oven setting is written on the arrow. A word equation is not enough, because it does not show the ratio of the molecules or the state of each substance. So we use symbols. After each substance we write its state: s for solid, like a precipitate or a powder. l for liquid. g for gas, like bubbles. v for vapour. And a q for aqueous, which means dissolved in water. On the arrow we write the conditions: the triangle means heat, cat means a catalyst, which speeds up a reaction without being used up, dil means dilute, and conc means concentrated. Fun fact: all metals are solid except mercury, the only liquid metal.
b4: The last branch, and the most important one: balancing. The scientist Lavoisier, the Father of Chemistry, said: nothing is lost and nothing is created. So the mass of the reactants is exactly equal to the mass of the products. That is why the scale in your book shows the same reading before and after the reaction. An equation has two kinds of numbers. The big number in front is the coefficient: the number of molecules. The small number below is the subscript: the number of atoms in one molecule. To count atoms, multiply them. Two H two O means four hydrogen atoms. And here is the golden rule: to balance an equation, change only the big numbers. Never touch the small ones, because if you change them, you change the substance itself!
